hook: Trusting your gut about people isn't a feeling. It's pattern recognition your brain finished before you caught up.
topic: The neuroscience of intuition — why gut feelings are real data
body:
**Trusting your gut about people isn't a feeling. It's pattern recognition your brain finished before you consciously caught up.**

Your nervous system has been reading human beings since long before you could speak. Facial expressions. Vocal tone. Whether someone's words and body are saying the same thing. The timing of when someone laughs. It has been building a database of behavioural patterns your entire life.

When you get that low hum of unease about someone — or that quiet sense of warmth and safety — that's not your imagination. That's your brain completing a pattern match and sending you a result. The signal arrives before the analysis because the analysis already happened, just below the threshold of conscious awareness.

The reason people dismiss it isn't because it's unreliable. It's because they have no framework to interpret it, so it just sits there feeling like anxiety, or projection, or overthinking.

But here's the crucial distinction: a genuine signal tends to be specific and quiet. It hums. It doesn't scream. Anxiety, by contrast, tends to be general — a vague, hovering dread that isn't attached to anything the other person actually did.

Learning to read people starts with learning to distinguish between those two things.

Start noticing: when you feel uneasy about someone, can you attach it to one specific thing they actually said or did? If yes — that's a signal worth paying attention to.

More on this in the link in my bio.
